en: He would die before his appointed death, she thought;
If Akbermet died,
Then he would see a day of consequence, she thought.
She had assembled extraordinary champions,
And had several warriors,
Looking farther beyond,
She had placed them there by magic.
Her tiger had borne twins;
None who met it returned alive.
Her leopard had borne twins;
None caught by it returned alive.
Her lion had borne twins;
None encountering it returned alive.
No human had ever gone there,
No two-legged mortal.
Farther on was more corruption,
Another marvel stood there:
It had a sword-shaped beak,
[It could strike and shatter a mountain,]
[And entering a forest, lay it flat.]
[No person could pass that way;]
[To the ill-fated, accursed creature,]
[No one who fell victim could survive.]
Knowing this, Akjoltoi
Had it placed there by magic.
Knowing its evil, Akjoltoi,
Fuming yet undaunted,
Whether fairy or giant,
In the end, the river-like sly Joltoi
Did not esteem it above his boot-top.
Toward the untrodden grey hill,
He turned Kulansur's head.
His figure appeared like a mountain,
Captivating the hearts of those who saw him;
He stood looking at the maidens.
The worthy man, proud as a rooster,
The unwavering worthy hero,
Thought that the hapless fairy maiden,
That radiant precious one,
Had crossed mountains on her journey,
And forded hard, weighty waters,
And had come seeking him;
She had abandoned the fairies' bazaar.
For brave Seytek's sake,
She had sought to satisfy her longing.
Unable to reach the grey-maned hero,
She had camped along the Broad Valley.
Because of the fire of love,
Many champions and myriad troops
Had been crushed along the road.
Thinking she might see days of happiness,
For Bermet who lived in this way,
Thinking what brave Seytek might do for her,
He drove his spear into the ground.
Unable to collect his thoughts,
His bewilderment burning fiercely,
And turned Kulansur's head.
Wondering at the fleeting world,
Sly Joltoi stood gazing.
The fairy maiden Akbermet—
The youngest of six daughters,
Her tent was of white silk;
Except for being a woman,
She was a champion among women.
When she reached eleven years,
Her father the sultan died.
When she reached thirteen,
And played at drawing the bow.
When she reached fourteen,
She understood the whole world
Through her wisdom.
When she reached fifteen,
She became sultan khan of the fairies,
And then Bermet mounted
Her father's golden throne.
When she reached eighteen,
She ruled in sovereign splendor.
Her multitude of fairies and many people
She governed without letting them stir.
Her father, the sultan padishah,
Had it built from precious stone:
With mirrors set into it,
Setting camel-sized jewels of ruby,
He had them lit in its brazier.
She entered it to sleep,
And when dawn approached,
All manner of things entered her dream.
Troubled in her sleep,
There appeared in her dream
A barefoot dervish.
The dervish stood and spoke to her,
Telling wonders no human had heard.
Listen to my words:
You are the daughter of the Fairy of Light,
The finest among women.
Understand the words I speak;
My child Akbermet, heed my counsel.
This is the decree written by God;
And listen carefully to my words.
The inheritor of truthful speech,
A descendant of the true Kyrgyz,
Blessed from his roots by Khizr.
His chief ancestors were all khans,
And Khizr blessed them all.
Their fortune surged and became a lake;
From the beginning they were grey-maned heroes.
When enemies emerged to fight them,
They leveled them with the black earth.
Cutting pain and grief.
His father's forefathers
Broke royal camps and took booty,
And attacked the peoples of the world.
Received their punishment by their hands.
They shattered mountains and made them level,
And acted, saying, We trust in fate.
And the enemies who blocked their way
They led the road on campaigns;
Descendant of Jobolong,
A saint named Kydyr,
Accompanied them as a companion.
His forefather was generous Manas the hero—
Youngest of the six heroes.
No such man appears in all the world.
Khizr's blessing came upon him,
And all the champions swiftly gathered;
Those who grappled with him were disgraced
And struck down upon the black earth.
Sacred Manas
Received wisdom from the unseen.
Unable to withstand his wrath,
The people of the Kagan submitted.
Think, my daughter, and hear this.
He is the descendant of Manas the tiger;
Hear the tale, my daughter.
This leopard is Manas's descendant;
Listen without grief.
Until the end of the age,
Though a plane tree be pierced, it does not pass away;
No soul passes without lamenting,
Who leaves this world without regret?
It is the Creator's decree;
Your husband until Judgment Day, he said,
And enter into delight,
Your lives joined in this life,
Your blood joined in one body.
When you play and rejoice, my master,
Seytek is your equal;
This is the man who will take you.
These are the saint's words;
He shares kinship with you,
And is himself the fairies' nephew.
Brave Seytek, the grey-maned hero,
Is the hero who will value your worth,
That young tiger of a man.
Your husband until Judgment Day, he said.
Lie upon the gilded bed
And enjoy its beauty, he said;
The champion whose hand you will hold.
This is the husband you will marry;
When they brought him for her to see,
His surge was like a rushing river,
And such was his heroic courage.
The chill streaming from his eyes
Was like flame in a bellows.
Broad-chested, with a proudly arched breast,
Such was the beauty of his form.
God knows whether it was true:
When I looked to his right,
There was a black-striped leopard,
Ready at once to tear a wound,
Crouching there to spring.
When I looked to his left,
There was a black-eared lion,
More wondrous than all the rest.
When I looked before him,
He bore the shape of a giant black bird;
Was the awe of a thousand champions.
Champion Seytek, the leopard,
Sword in hand,
He loomed over the ridgeline,
Glowering with eyes wide.
Beside him were about forty companions,
Enough to guard the whole world.
Let alone a human, he looked able
To drink the blood of a lion outright.
If he grew wrathful, the black earth
Seemed barely able to bear his multitude.
If he poured out his wrath upon the world,
He could leave it desolate.
My distracted thoughts—
In my dream I saw this troubling deed,
I saw such inexhaustible strength.
His eyes were burning embers;
When I saw his bodily form,
My tiny soul cried out,
And my tiny life trembled,
I prayed to the true God.
Love burned in flame,
Into my bones, not only my flesh.
Seeing his beauty, I marveled,
Lamenting, My grey-maned hero,
Seeing him, I marveled,
And yearned at the sight of his figure.
My early words had become late;
To reach brave Seytek,
My two eyes became four with longing.
Broad-chested and radiant-faced,
His form differed from every other soul;
He had come into creation,
With a human form unlike all others.
He himself was eighteen years old,
With the appearance of a hero from birth.
He wore a golden belt,
And moonlight covered his face.
He stood unsmiling and solemn.
Seeing him captivated the heart,
He appeared to my eyes as a master;
If by chance he surged in fury,
No mountain could withstand him.
Seeing him, my heart was captivated:
Tears spilling from my eyes,
My many thoughts scattered one by one.
My fleshly heart trembled;
In my dream I saw such a man.
Only a spoonful of our blood remained;
Our strength had grown feeble.
When I looked again upon his form,
My heart surged and wandered,
This yawning ravine
Seemed formed from his throat;
Driving the whole world before him,
He seemed born to be its support.
Seeing this, I marveled,
Lamenting and imploring God:
God, grant him firmly to me,
I prayed, distraught.
While sleeping in my dream,
I fell into the fire of love.
As I stood there astonished,
Four men came beside me.
When I asked who the four were,
One was Khizr and one was Fortune;
One was Prosperity and one was Wisdom,
Standing before me.
You were a princess and padishah among fairies.
Your grey-maned husband who opens fortune, they said.
The dark grey-maned Seytek
Was suddenly brought before me.
Facing the qibla, they recited the marriage rite,
My heart burned and my blood boiled,
My heart surged and my eyes shone,
The pleasures of this world
Where is your lineage and fame? I asked,
Questioning him as I clung to him.
When I questioned him, he spoke,
And told many tales:
